{{Short description|American biologist}}
'''Jeffery Lee Dangl''' (born October 13, 1957) is an American biologist and geneticist whose research concerns plant immunity<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dangl |first1=Jeffery L. |last2=Jones |first2=Jonathan D. G. |date=2024-12-20 |title=A common immune response node in diverse plants |journal=Science |publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science |volume=386 |issue=6728 |pages=1344–1346 |doi=10.1126/science.adu4930|doi-access=free |pmid=39700299 |bibcode=2024Sci...386.1344D }}</ref>, plant–microbe interactions, [[molecular genetics]], and plant-associated microbiomes.<ref>{{Cite web |last=McCormack |first=Joshua |date=2025-06-10 |title=Serendipity shaped this biologist's research career {{!}} UNC-Chapel Hill |url=https://www.unc.edu/posts/2025/06/10/serendipity-shaped-this-biologists-research-career/ |access-date=2026-09-25 |website=The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill |language=en-US}}</ref> He is the John N. Couch Distinguished Professor of Biology at the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]] (UNC) and an investigator of the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]]. He is a Foreign Member of the [[Royal Society]] and an elected member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]], the [[German National Academy of Sciences Leopoldina]], and the [[American Academy of Microbiology]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Azar |first=Beth |date=2010-07-27 |title=Profile of Jeffery L. Dangl |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=107 |issue=30 |pages=13203–13205 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1008172107 |doi-access=free |pmc=2922171 |pmid=20615942 |bibcode=2010PNAS..10713203A }}</ref>

Dangl's research has contributed to the molecular understanding of [[Innate immune system|plant innate immunity]]<ref>{{Cite news |last=Manning |first=Anne |date=2019-08-22 |title=Experiments illuminate key component of plants' immune systems |url=https://natsci.source.colostate.edu/experiments-illuminate-key-component-of-plants-immune-systems/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240603090452/https://natsci.source.colostate.edu/experiments-illuminate-key-component-of-plants-immune-systems/ |archive-date=2024-06-03 |access-date=2026-09-25 |work=College of Natural Sciences |language=en-US}}</ref>, including [[Disease resistance|disease-resistance genes]], [[Immune receptor|intracellular immune receptors]], pathogen effectors, and the interactions between plants and their associated microbial communities. With [[Jonathan D. G. Jones]], he developed the "zigzag model" of plant immunity, a conceptual framework describing the evolutionary interaction between plant immune responses and pathogen virulence mechanisms.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1038/nature05286 | title = The plant immune system | year = 2006 | last1 = Jones | first1 = J. D. G. | authorlink1 = Jonathan D. G. Jones| last2 = Dangl | first2 = J. L. | authorlink2 = Jeffery Dangl| journal = [[Nature (journal)|Nature]] | volume = 444 | pages = 323–9| pmid = 17108957 | issue = 7117 |bibcode = 2006Natur.444..323J | doi-access = free }}</ref>

In 2025, Dangl shared the [[Wolf Prize in Agriculture]] with Jones and [[Brian Staskawicz|Brian J. Staskawicz]] for groundbreaking discoveries concerning the immune system and disease resistance in plants.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-03-10 |title=Jonathan Jones becomes TSL's 2nd Wolf Prize Laureate |url=https://www.tsl.ac.uk/news/jonathan-jones-becomes-tsls-2nd-wolf-prize-laureate |access-date=2026-09-25 |website=The Sainsbury Laboratory |language=en}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
He grew up in [[Redding, California]]. He attended [[Stanford University]], where he received undergraduate degrees in Biological Sciences and Modern Literature in 1981.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Azar |first=Beth |date=2010-07-27 |title=Profile of jeffery L. Dangl |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=107 |issue=30 |pages=13203–13205 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1008172107 |doi-access=free |issn=1091-6490 |pmc=2922171 |pmid=20615942 |bibcode=2010PNAS..10713203A }}</ref> He received his PhD. from the [[Stanford University School of Medicine]] in 1986 under the supervision of [[Leonard Herzenberg|Leonard A. Herzenberg]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dangl |first1=Jeffery L. |last2=Lanier |first2=Lewis L. |date=2013-12-24 |title=Founding father of FACS: Professor Leonard A. Herzenberg (1931–2013) |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=110 |issue=52 |pages=20848–20849 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1321731111 |doi-access=free |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=3876245 |pmid=24344298 |bibcode=2013PNAS..11020848D }}</ref> His doctoral research concerned genetically engineered chimeric monoclonal antibodies and somatically selected mouse immunoglobulin [[Heavy chain disease|heavy-chain genes]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Spotlight Q & A with Professor Jeff Dangl |url=https://www.2blades.org/newsroom/spotlight-jeff-dangl |access-date=2026-09-25 |website=2Blades |date=3 September 2025 |language=en-US}}</ref>

Dangl's early research was in [[mammalian immunology]]. His work included studies of mouse immunoglobulin genes and antibody structure. A 1986 paper in ''Nature'', co-authored with researchers from Stanford and other institutions, examined recombination involving an expressed mouse immunoglobulin heavy-chain gene.

He subsequently conducted postdoctoral research with Klaus Hahlbrock at the [[Max Planck Institute for Plant Breeding Research]] in Cologne, Germany. During this period he shifted his research focus from mammalian immunology to plant molecular biology and plant–pathogen interactions. In 1989, he established an independent research group at the Max Delbrück Laboratory in [[Cologne]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Roots and microbes: Bringing a complex underground ecology into the lab |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2012/08/120801132440.htm |access-date=2026-09-25 |website=ScienceDaily |language=en}}</ref>

==Career==
In 1995, Dangl joined the faculty of the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]]. He holds appointments in the Department of Biology and the Department of Microbiology and Immunology and is a member of the university's genetics and genomics programs. He subsequently became the John N. Couch Distinguished Professor of Biology and, in 2011,  an investigator of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute.<ref>{{Cite web |last=McCormack |first=Joshua |date=2025-06-10 |title=Serendipity shaped this biologist's research career {{!}} UNC-Chapel Hill |url=https://www.unc.edu/posts/2025/06/10/serendipity-shaped-this-biologists-research-career/ |access-date=2026-09-25 |website=The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill |language=en-US}}</ref>

Dangl has served on scientific and governmental advisory bodies, including the [[National Research Council (United States)|National Research Council]]'s Board on Life Sciences. He chaired and contributed to National Research Council reviews concerning the National Plant Genome Research Initiative and participated in advisory and review activities for national research agencies.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Professor Dr Jeff L. Dangl |url=https://www.leopoldina.org/en/members/member-list/detail/jeff-l-dangl |access-date=2026-09-25 |website=www.leopoldina.org}}</ref>

== Research ==

=== Plant immunity ===
Dangl's research established [[Plant Molecular Biology|plant molecular]] genetics as a major approach to studying innate immunity and plant–pathogen interactions.<ref name=":2" /> His laboratory contributed to the development of ''[[Arabidopsis thaliana]]'' as a model for investigating plant disease resistance and helped identify molecular components involved in pathogen recognition and immune signalling.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Koornneef |first1=Maarten |last2=Meinke |first2=David |date=2010 |title=The development of Arabidopsis as a model plant |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1365-313X.2009.04086.x |journal=The Plant Journal |language=en |volume=61 |issue=6 |pages=909–921 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-313X.2009.04086.x |pmid=20409266 |bibcode=2010PlJ....61..909K |issn=1365-313X}}</ref>

A major focus of his research has been plant disease-resistance genes and nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) proteins. These intracellular immune receptors detect pathogen-derived molecules or changes caused by pathogen effectors and activate defensive responses. Dangl's research has contributed to understanding the molecular mechanisms by which these receptors recognize pathogen activity and initiate immune signalling.<ref name=":1" />

Together with Jonathan D. G. Jones, Dangl developed the zigzag model of [[plant immunity]], introduced in a 2006 ''Nature'' review. The model integrates pattern-triggered immunity, [[pathogen]] effector-mediated suppression of host defence, and effector-triggered immunity mediated by intracellular immune receptors. It was proposed as a conceptual framework for understanding the coevolution between plant resistance mechanisms and pathogen virulence factors. Subsequent reviews have described the Jones–Dangl zigzag model as a widely used framework for explaining plant–pathogen interactions.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Jones |first1=Jonathan D. G. |last2=Dangl |first2=Jeffery L. |date=2006 |title=The plant immune system |url=https://doi.org/10.1038/nature05286 |journal=Nature |volume=444 |issue=7117 |pages=323–329 |doi=10.1038/nature05286 |pmid=17108957 |bibcode=2006Natur.444..323J |issn=0028-0836}}</ref>

=== Plant microbiomes ===
Later work in the Dangl laboratory expanded from [[pathogen]] recognition to the broader community of microorganisms associated with plants. The laboratory pioneered research into the organization and function of [[Plant community|plant-associated]] [[microbiomes]], investigating how plants distinguish beneficial microorganisms from pathogens and how immune signalling influences microbial communities.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Roots and Microbes: Bringing a Complex Underground Ecology into the Lab {{!}} HHMI |url=https://www.hhmi.org/news/roots-and-microbes-bringing-complex-underground-ecology-lab |access-date=2026-09-25 |website=www.hhmi.org |language=en}}</ref>

In a 2017 ''Nature'' study, Dangl and colleagues investigated how [[Root microbiome|root microbiota]] interact with [[Plant nutrition|plant nutrient]] responses and immunity, finding that the genetic network controlling phosphate stress influenced the composition of the [[Root microbiome|root microbial]] community.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Castrillo |first1=Gabriel |last2=Teixeira |first2=Paulo José Pereira Lima |last3=Paredes |first3=Sur Herrera |last4=Law |first4=Theresa F. |last5=de Lorenzo |first5=Laura |last6=Feltcher |first6=Meghan E. |last7=Finkel |first7=Omri M. |last8=Breakfield |first8=Natalie W. |last9=Mieczkowski |first9=Piotr |last10=Jones |first10=Corbin D. |last11=Paz-Ares |first11=Javier |last12=Dangl |first12=Jeffery L. |date=2017-03-23 |title=Root microbiota drive direct integration of phosphate stress and immunity |journal=Nature |volume=543 |issue=7646 |pages=513–518 |doi=10.1038/nature21417 |issn=1476-4687 |pmc=5364063 |pmid=28297714 |bibcode=2017Natur.543..513C }}</ref>

Dangl subsequently co-authored a 2019 review, ''Beyond pathogens: microbiota interactions with the plant immune system'', which examined interactions between [[Plant disease resistance|plant immune systems]] and beneficial or [[Microorganisms|commensal microorganisms]].<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last1=Teixeira |first1=Paulo José PL |last2=Colaianni |first2=Nicholas R |last3=Fitzpatrick |first3=Connor R |last4=Dangl |first4=Jeffery L |date=2019 |title=Beyond pathogens: microbiota interactions with the plant immune system |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S1369527419300396 |journal=Current Opinion in Microbiology |language=en |volume=49 |pages=7–17 |doi=10.1016/j.mib.2019.08.003 |pmid=31563068 |bibcode=2019COMb...49....7T }}</ref>

His laboratory has also contributed to research on the [[plant microbiome]] at the level of [[microbial ecology]] and [[Memory|molecular mechanisms]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=mlballon |date=2017-12-18 |title=A Functional Genomics Database for Plant Microbiome Studies |url=https://archive.jgi.doe.gov/functional-genomics-database-for-plant-microbiome-studies/ |access-date=2026-09-25 |website=Archive |language=en-US}}</ref> A 2020 ''[[Annual Review of Microbiology]]'' article co-authored by Dangl examined the development of plant microbiome research from ecological studies toward mechanistic and reductionist approaches.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last1=Fitzpatrick |first1=Connor R. |last2=Salas-González |first2=Isai |last3=Conway |first3=Jonathan M. |last4=Finkel |first4=Omri M. |last5=Gilbert |first5=Sarah |last6=Russ |first6=Dor |last7=Teixeira |first7=Paulo José Pereira Lima |last8=Dangl |first8=Jeffery L. |date=2020 |title=The Plant Microbiome: From Ecology to Reductionism and Beyond |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-micro-022620-014327 |journal=Annual Review of Microbiology |publisher=Annual Reviews |volume=74 |pages=81–100 |doi=10.1146/annurev-micro-022620-014327 |pmid=32530732 |issn=1545-3251}}</ref>

More recent research from the laboratory has examined [[microbial metabolism]] and plant-associated bacterial communities, including studies of bacterial auxin [[catabolism]] in the [[plant microbiome]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Conway |first1=Jonathan M. |last2=Walton |first2=William G. |last3=Salas-González |first3=Isai |last4=Law |first4=Theresa F. |last5=Lindberg |first5=Chloe A. |last6=Crook |first6=Laura E. |last7=Kosina |first7=Suzanne M. |last8=Fitzpatrick |first8=Connor R. |last9=Lietzan |first9=Adam D. |last10=Northen |first10=Trent R. |last11=Jones |first11=Corbin D. |last12=Finkel |first12=Omri M. |last13=Redinbo |first13=Matthew R. |last14=Dangl |first14=Jeffery L. |date=2022-10-20 |title=Diverse MarR bacterial regulators of auxin catabolism in the plant microbiome |journal=Nature Microbiology |language=en |volume=7 |issue=11 |pages=1817–1833 |doi=10.1038/s41564-022-01244-3 |issn=2058-5276 |pmc=9613470 |pmid=36266335}}</ref>

=== Connections to animal innate immunity ===
Dangl's research on plant immune receptors has also contributed to broader comparisons between plant and animal [[Innate immune system|innate immune systems]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hunter |first=Philip |date=2005 |title=Common defences |journal=EMBO Reports |volume=6 |issue=6 |pages=504–507 |doi=10.1038/sj.embor.7400439 |issn=1469-221X |pmc=1369097 |pmid=15940281}}</ref> Plant NLR proteins share structural and functional characteristics with intracellular immune receptors in animals. Human NOD proteins, for example, belong to a broader family of intracellular immune proteins related to plant disease-resistance proteins.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Stewart |first=Melissa |date=2015-09-24 |title=Bye-bye, Bugs: Jeff Dangl is UNC's plant disease-buster |url=https://magazine.college.unc.edu/features/dangl/ |access-date=2026-09-25 |website=Carolina Arts & Sciences Magazine |language=en-US}}</ref>

This relationship became particularly relevant to human disease research after mutations in the human ''NOD2'' gene were associated with susceptibility to [[Crohn's disease]]. The discovery established a connection between the molecular architecture of plant disease-resistance proteins and mechanisms of innate immune recognition in animals.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nishimura |first1=Marc T. |last2=Dangl |first2=Jeffery L. |date=2010 |title=Arabidopsis and the plant immune system |journal=The Plant Journal |language=en |volume=61 |issue=6 |pages=1053–1066 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-313X.2010.04131.x |issn=0960-7412 |pmc=2859471 |pmid=20409278 |bibcode=2010PlJ....61.1053N }}</ref> Dangl's work on [[Plant defense against herbivory|plant resistance genes]] and [[Immune receptor|immune receptors]] formed part of the broader scientific context for comparative studies of these immune systems.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-04-26 |title=50 Years of Plant Immunity Breakthroughs |url=https://www.tsl.ac.uk/news/50-years-of-plant-immunity-breakthroughs |access-date=2026-09-25 |website=The Sainsbury Laboratory |language=en}}</ref>

The relationship should not be described as Dangl having discovered the genetic cause of Crohn's disease; rather, his research contributed to understanding the plant immune-receptor systems that provided an important comparative framework for subsequent research on related animal innate immune proteins.<ref name=":3" />

== Editorial and advisory work ==
Dangl has served on the editorial boards of several scientific journals. He has served on the editorial boards of [[Science (journal)|''Science'']], [[Cell (journal)|''Cell'']], and ''[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]'', and has held editorial responsibilities for ''Current Opinion in Plant Biology''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Editorial board - Current Opinion in Plant Biology {{!}} ScienceDirect.com by Elsevier |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/current-opinion-in-plant-biology/about/editorial-board |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231010133827/https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/current-opinion-in-plant-biology/about/editorial-board |archive-date=2023-10-10 |access-date=2026-09-25 |website=www.sciencedirect.com |language=en-us}}</ref>

He has also participated in scientific advisory activities outside academia. Dangl is a member of the Scientific Advisory Board of [[2Blades]], an organization working on [[plant immunity]] and [[Plant disease|crop disease]] resistance.<ref name=":2" /> 

== Awards and honours ==

Dangl was elected a member of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 2004. He was elected to the [[German National Academy of Sciences Leopoldina]] in 2003, the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 2007, and the [[American Academy of Microbiology]] in 2011.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.aspb.org/committees/hales.cfm |title=Stephen Hales Prize |access-date=2009-04-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090110123626/http://www.aspb.org/committees/hales.cfm |archive-date=2009-01-10 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="NationalAcademyWebsite">[https://web.archive.org/web/20110604025010/http://www.nasonline.org/site/Dir/1714335241?pg=vprof&mbr=1010560&returl=http:%2F%2Fwww.nasonline.org%2Fsite%2FDir%2F1714335241%3Fpg=srch&view=basic&retmk=search_again_link National Academy of Sciences Page]</ref>

In 2023, Dangl was elected a [[Foreign Member of the Royal Society]] (ForMemRS), the United Kingdom's national academy of sciences.<ref>{{cite web |title=Professor Jeffery Dangl ForMemRS |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/jeff-dangl-36197 |publisher=The Royal Society |access-date=22 September 2026}}</ref>

He has received the Stephen Hales Prize from the [[American Society of Plant Biologists]] and an award from the [[International Society for Molecular Plant-Microbe Interactions]] for contributions to the understanding of plant–pathogen interactions.<ref name="pnas">{{Cite journal

In 2025, Dangl shared the [[Wolf Prize in Agriculture]] with Jonathan D. G. Jones and Brian J. Staskawicz.<ref>[https://wolffund.org.il/jeffery-l-dangl/ Wolf Prize 2025 in Agriculture]</ref> 

==Personal life==
Dangl has a rare form of [[muscular dystrophy]], [[facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy]].<ref name="pnas" /> Dangl is married to biologist Sarah Grant.<ref name="pnas" /><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Marx |first=Vivien |date=2013-10-01 |title=Jeff Dangl |journal=Nature Methods |language=en |volume=10 |issue=10 |pages=919 |doi=10.1038/nmeth.2653 |pmid=24161968 |s2cid=205422081 |issn=1548-7105|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dangl |first=Jeffrey L. |date=2014-06-01 |title=Interview with Jeffrey L. Dangl |url=https://www.cell.com/trends/plant-science/abstract/S1360-1385(14)00092-2 |journal=Trends in Plant Science |language=English |volume=19 |issue=6 |pages=342–343 |doi=10.1016/j.tplants.2014.04.003 |issn=1360-1385 |pmid=24794128|bibcode=2014TPS....19..342D |url-access=subscription }}</ref>
